q: 1. The resultant stress on an inclined plane which is inclined at an angle θ to the normal cross-section... is
explain: The resultant stress on a plane inclined at θ is the vector sum of normal and tangential stress, which simplifies to σ cosθ for a single axial stress.

q: 2. When a body is subjected to a direct tensile stress (σ) in one plane, then maximum normal stress occurs at a section inclined at
explain: Normal stress is σ cos²θ. This is maximum when cos θ = 1, which occurs at θ = 0° (the plane perpendicular to the force).

q: 3. A body is subjected to a direct tensile stress (σ) in one plane. The shear stress is maximum at a section inclined at ............ to the normal of the section.
explain: Shear stress is (σ/2) sin 2θ. This is maximum when sin 2θ = 1 (at 2θ = 90° or 270°), giving θ = 45° and 135°.

q: 4. When a body is subjected to a direct tensile stress (σ) in one plane, the maximum shear stress is ............ the maximum normal stress.
explain: Maximum normal stress is σ (at 0°), and maximum shear stress is σ/2 (at 45°). Therefore, max shear is half of max normal stress.

q: 5. Principle plane is a plane on which the shear stress is
explain: Principal planes are defined as planes where the shear stress component is zero.

q: 6. In Mohr's circle, the centre of circle from Y-axis is taken as
explain: The center of the Mohr's circle on the σ-axis is always the average of the two normal stresses: (σx + σy)/2.

q: 7. The energy stored in a body when strained within elastic limit is known as
explain: Strain energy is the internal work done by the force to deform a body, stored as potential energy while within the elastic limit.

q: 8. The total strain energy stored in a body is termed as
explain: Resilience is the total strain energy stored in a body within its elastic limit.

q: 9. Strain energy is the
options: energy stored in a body when strained within elastic limits
energy stored in a body when strained upto the breaking of a specimen
maximum strain energy which can be stored in a body
proof resilience per unit volume of a material
explain: As defined in Q. 327, it is the energy absorbed by a material when it is deformed elastically.

q: 10. Resilience is the
options: energy stored in a body when strained within elastic limits
energy stored in a body when strained upto the breaking of the specimen
maximum strain energy which can be stored in a body
explain: as per key d Resilience is the general capacity of a material to absorb energy when it is deformed elastically and release that energy upon unloading.

q: 11. The stress induced in a body, when suddenly loaded, is ............ the stress induced when the same load is applied gradually.
explain: For a suddenly applied load, the instantaneous stress reached is twice the value of the static stress produced by the same load.

q: 12. The strain energy stored in a spring, when subjected to maximum load, without suffering permanent distortion, is known as
explain: Proof resilience is the maximum strain energy a body can store without undergoing permanent (plastic) deformation.

q: 13. The capacity of a strained body for doing work on the removal of the straining force, is called
explain: This is another definition of resilience, emphasizing the ability to return to the original state and release stored energy.

q: 14. If the strains in the three principal directions are εx, εy and εz, the volumetric strain will be
explain: Volumetric strain (e_v) is the sum of the linear strains in three mutually perpendicular directions.

q: 15. In a stressed body the minimum normal stress at any point is always
options: average of two normal stresses acting in the two principal directions
difference of two normal stresses in the two principal directions plus shear stresses on those planes
explain: As noted in Q. 340, both the maximum and minimum normal stresses are referred to as principal stresses.

q: 16. The maximum shear stress will be equal to
options: one half of the algebraic difference of the maximum and minimum principal stresses at the point
the intensity of shear stress acting on the major principal plane
the shear stress acting on the planes in the direction of two principal directions
explain: τ_max = (σ1 - σ2) / 2, where σ1 and σ2 are the major and minor principal stresses.

q: 17. The ratio of strengths of a rivet in double shear to that in a single shear will be
explain: In double shear, there are two planes resisting the shear force, effectively doubling the strength compared to a single shear plane.

q: 18. An isotropic material is the one which
options: has same structure at all the points
has Young's modulus equal to modulus of rigidity
has the elastic constants, identical in all the directions
explain: As established in Q. 277, isotropic materials exhibit the same elastic properties regardless of the direction of measurement.

q: 19. When a member is subjected to a twisting moment, the material will be subjected to ............
explain: Torsion creates internal resistance in the form of shear stresses that act on the cross-sectional planes and longitudinal planes.

q: 20. When a member is subjected to twisting moment the stress in any elemental ring will be proportional to ............
options: Modulus of rigidity of the material
explain: According to the torsion formula $\frac{\tau}{r} = \frac{T}{J}$, shear stress ($\tau$) is directly proportional to the radial distance ($r$) from the center.

q: 21. In a shaft subjected to pure torsion, maximum shear stress will occur at ............
options: a distance of semi-radius from centre
explain: Since shear stress is proportional to the radius ($r$), it is zero at the center and reaches its maximum value at the outer boundary (periphery) where $r=R$.

q: 22. What are the units of torque?
explain: Torque is defined as Force $\times$ perpendicular distance, hence its SI unit is Newton-meter (Nm).

q: 23. The torsional formula is valid if the shearing stresses ............
options: are within the shearing proportional limit
are caused due to twisting moment applied only at the free end
explain: The torsion formula assumes linear elastic behavior, meaning the shear stress must be within the proportional limit of the material.

q: 24. The diamond quadrilateral pyramid indenter is used in ............
explain: The Vickers hardness test uses a square-based diamond pyramid indenter with an angle of 136° between opposite faces.

q: 25. In Brinell Hardness test, the type of indenter used is ............
explain: The Brinell test uses a hardened steel (or tungsten carbide) ball of a specified diameter (usually 10mm) as the indenter.

q: 26. Glass will obey Hooke's law upto ............
explain: Glass is a perfectly brittle material. It shows almost no plastic deformation and fails (fractures) suddenly while still in the linear elastic range.

q: 27. The proportional limit of mild steel specimen is taken as the stress corresponding to a permanent set of ............
explain: While proof stress is often 0.2%, the limit of proportionality is very sensitive and is often associated with a very small permanent set like 0.01%.

q: 28. Within the elastic range of a tensile test the deviation from Hooke's law and some after effects may be noticed. This is due to ............
options: material does not at all obey Hooke's law
elastic limit is greater than ultimate strength
explain: Thermo-elastic effects involve small temperature changes during loading/unloading that can cause slight non-linearity even within the elastic range.

q: 29. The compression test is commonly used for testing ............
explain: Brittle materials (like concrete, cast iron, or stone) are much stronger in compression than tension, making compression tests standard for them.

q: 30. When a cylindrical specimen of a ductile material is subjected to compression ............
options: it ultimately assumes the shape of a flat disc
it fails by fracture like a brittle material
it fails immediately after starting of loading
explain: Ductile materials under compression undergo significant plastic deformation (bulging) without fracturing, eventually flattening into a disc shape.

q: 31. What is strain energy?
options: the energy stored in a body because of being strained
the energy that is spent for straining a body
explain: Strain energy is the internal work done by external forces while deforming a body, which is stored as potential energy.

q: 32. The strain energy stored in a body due to an axial stress is ............
explain: The formula for strain energy ($U$) under axial load is $U = \frac{\sigma^2}{2E} \times V$.

q: 33. Strain energy due to bending stress is ............
explain: For a beam subjected to a bending moment $M$, the total strain energy is obtained by integrating $\frac{M^2}{2EI}$ over the length of the beam.

q: 34. What is the core of a section ............
options: portion where a compressive force applied causes no tension anywhere
the central portion of the cross-section of similar shape but half the area
area where compressive force will not cause any compressive stress
explain: The 'core' or 'kern' is the area within which an eccentric load can be applied without inducing any tensile stress in the section.

q: 35. To avoid any possibility of tension occurring in masonry structures, the resultant of various forces at any level must pass through ............
options: middle third of the width or depth of the section
explain: For rectangular sections (like masonry walls), the 'middle-third rule' states that the resultant must stay within the middle third to prevent tension.

q: 36. The ratio of the moment of inertia of a circular plate and that of a square plate for equal depth, is ............
explain: For depth (dimension) 'd': I(circle) = πd⁴/64, I(square) = d⁴/12. Ratio = (πd⁴/64) / (d⁴/12) = 12π/64 = 3π/16.

q: 37. The intensity of direct longitudinal stress in the cross-section at any point distant r from the neutral axis, is proportional to ............
explain: According to the bending equation (M/I = σ/y), the bending stress (σ) is directly proportional to the distance (y or r) from the neutral axis.

q: 38. The limit of eccentricity for no tensile conditions for a column of circular section of diameter (d) is ............
explain: To ensure no tension at any point in a circular section, the load must fall within the middle quarter of the diameter, meaning the eccentricity e ≤ d/8.

q: 39. In a tensile test, when the material is stressed beyond elastic limit, the tensile strain ............ as compared to the stress.
explain: Beyond the elastic limit (in the plastic region), the material undergoes large deformations for very small increments in stress.

q: 40. The breaking stress is ............ the ultimate stress.
explain: In a nominal stress-strain curve for ductile materials, 'necking' occurs after the ultimate stress, causing the load (and nominal stress) to drop before breaking.

q: 41. The ratio of the largest load in a test to the original cross-sectional area of the test piece is called ............
explain: Ultimate tensile strength (UTS) is defined as the maximum load reached during the test divided by the original area.

q: 42. A tensile test is performed on a mild steel round bar. Its diameter after fracture will ............
explain: Mild steel is ductile; before it breaks, it undergoes 'necking,' which is a localized reduction in the cross-sectional area.

q: 43. A tensile test is performed on a round bar. After fracture it has been found that the diameter remains approximately same at fracture. The material under test was ............
explain: Cast iron is a brittle material. It fails by sudden fracture with very little plastic deformation or necking, so the diameter remains nearly unchanged.

q: 44. In compression test, the fracture in cast iron specimen would occur along ............
options: at right angles to the axis of specimen
explain: Brittle materials in compression often fail due to shear on an oblique plane (typically around 45 degrees) because they are weaker in shear than in pure compression.

q: 45. A column that fails primarily due to direct stress is called
explain: Short columns fail by crushing (direct compressive stress) rather than buckling.

q: 46. For keeping the stress wholly compressive, the load may be applied on a circular column anywhere within a concentric circle of diameter
explain: The kern of a solid circular section of diameter d is a concentric circle of diameter d/4.

q: 47. A truss is completely analyzed, when
options: the direct stress in all the members are found
all the external reactions components are determined
explain: A truss analysis is complete once the axial (direct) force/stress in every member has been determined.

q: 48. A tie is a member which
options: is subjected to axial compression only
is subjected to axial tension only
is subjected to moment tension only
is subjected to two equal and opposite forces
explain: A tie carries axial tension only, as opposed to a strut which carries compression.

q: 49. In simple bending theory, the assumption that plane section before bending remains plane after bending implies that
options: stress is proportional to strain at all sections
strain is proportional to the distance from the natural axis
stress is uniform in the cross-section
explain: The plane-sections assumption directly implies a linear strain distribution across the depth, proportional to distance from the neutral axis.

q: 50. If a beam is loaded transversely, the maximum compressive stress develops on
explain: For typical sagging (downward transverse load), the top fiber is in maximum compression.
